claims.text: Suspect several substances when an adult self-poisons on purpose.
claims.quote: If purposeful self-poisoning occurs in adults, multiple substances should be suspected.

claims.text: Always consider a suicide attempt in older children, adolescents and adults who ingest a drug.
claims.quote: Attempted suicide must always be considered in older children, adolescents, and adults who have ingested a drug or medication

claims.text: Acetaminophen level in every mixed ingestion: it is common, often silent early, and its delayed toxicity can be prevented with an antidote.
claims.quote: Many authorities recommend measuring acetaminophen levels in all patients with mixed ingestions because acetaminophen ingestion is common, is often asymptomatic during the early stages, and can cause serious delayed toxicity that can be prevented by an antidote.

claims.text: Levels that can guide treatment: acetaminophen, aspirin, carbon monoxide, digoxin, ethylene glycol, iron, lithium, methanol, phenobarbital, phenytoin, theophylline.
claims.quote: For a few substances (eg, acetaminophen, aspirin, carbon monoxide, digoxin, ethylene glycol, iron, lithium, methanol, phenobarbital, phenytoin, theophylline), blood levels may help guide treatment.

claims.text: Electrolytes, BUN, creatinine, glucose, coagulation studies and VBG with altered consciousness or abnormal vital signs.
claims.quote: For patients who have altered consciousness or abnormal vital signs or who have ingested certain substances, laboratory tests may include serum electrolytes, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), creatinine, glucose, coagulation studies, and venous blood gases (VBGs).

claims.text: ECG and cardiac monitoring for drugs with cardiovascular effects or an unknown substance.
claims.quote: For poisonings with drugs or medications that have cardiovascular effects or with an unknown substance, electrocardiography (ECG) and cardiac monitoring are indicated.

claims.text: Urine drug screens are qualitative and limited.
claims.quote: Standard, readily available urine or blood tests to identify common drugs of abuse (often called toxic screens) are qualitative, not quantitative.

claims.text: The opioid immunoassay misses fentanyl and methadone.
claims.quote: For example, an opioid urine immunoassay test does not detect fentanyl or methadone but does react with very small amounts of morphine or codeine analogues.

claims.text: Serum osmolality, methemoglobin, carbon monoxide level or brain CT for certain suspected poisons.
claims.quote: Other tests (eg, serum osmolality, methemoglobin level, carbon monoxide level, brain CT) may be indicated for certain suspected poisons or in certain clinical situations.
